description: The challenge is to create an interactive game that allows players to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission, teaching them about the engineering decisions involved in real-world space exploration.
summary:
PRIORITY SEVEN is a board game that we developed for 1-4 players about one of the most difficult things in space mission that usually gets leftout, which is getting data back to Earth. Players are to design a robotic Mars mission, first picking different features such as robots, onboard memory, cruise stage and antenna and then run it for 12 weeks/rounds. Each player picks a seat at mission control and all players then share a shared pool of 8 Action Points (AP), meaning for a player to be doing something ambitios, another one has to do less.
Robots collect data every round but if it doesn't reach the Earth it doesn't count, and to send it you need time on one of the 14 antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network with ~60 other missions. Each round, the team requests time and negotiates for it, and in case of disagreement just like in how real networks settle conflicts you have to have a better alternative. A board game models this process better than software as it simulates the real process of people arguing with each other.
At some point in the game as deadlines come, players are forced to decide which science to give up on. This mimics what Galileo's team did when its antenna failed, returnign ~70% of their planned objectives. 
Event cards include incidents, figures from NASA and JPL sources, cited on each card. Equipment and objective values (costs, masses, capacities) are game-design numbers, tuned by simulation.
details:
Priority Seven is a browser board game about getting the data back to Earth, which is one of the main things that from our research most games skip. NASA's Deep Space Network 14 antennas are overloaded with missions reaching ~60 so the science of the mission only counts when it actually is dowloaded.

4 Players take the roles of Explorer, Researcher, Engineer and Flight Director. You have to design a Mars mission, pick different things it will include (rover, orbiter, helicopter, antenna, radio band, recorder), then operate and run it for 12 weeks/rounds. Each week you reuest antenna slots against missions of rivals, you also cannot refuse a conflict, you can only counter-propose, just like in real DSN negotiations. Robots fill their records faster than what the link can empty and and event card is drawn every round. When a deadline can't be met, you have to withdraw an objective. The game doesn't really have a win screen, instead after each mission you get a report/debreef of which objectives were returned, dark, unusable or withdrawn. The report ends with the score comparison to Galileo, whose high-gain antenna failed to open, being expected to keep up 70% of its science.

Real data: the game includes weekly Earth-Mars distance from JPL Horizons which sets the amount of cards each antenna slot carries. Photos come from NASA image and Video Library, flare records from DONKI, and asteroid elements from the Small-Body Database. DSN size, load and scheduling rules come from NASA OIG audit and a JPL scheduling paper. We also tagged every number in the game as either DATA, DERIVED or MODEL, so players can see what was our game choice and what is actual published data.

Benefit and impact: players will learn why bandwidth, not hardware, limits space science and that the ground and user segments matter as much as the spacecraft itself.

The game is built with HTML, CSS and Java Script and hosted on Github pages. It also is in one single file with no backend. The game can be played with a keyboard only, the audio-only mode can turn the board into sound too.

Limit is that we have not run group playtests.
